name: Cornelius Vanderbilt

summary.text: Cornelius Vanderbilt was the New York shipping and railroad financier who in 1868 attempted to buy control of the Erie Railroad and was met by the issuance of new Erie shares by directors Daniel Drew, Jay Gould and James Fisk, an episode known as the Erie War. Histories report he lost several million dollars in the attempt before a settlement.

facts.claim: In February 1868 the Erie Railroad board, controlled by Daniel Drew, Jay Gould and James Fisk, authorized about $5 million in convertible bonds that were quickly exchanged for new shares, diluting Cornelius Vanderbilt's attempt to buy control of the road.
facts.quote: Drew, Gould, and Fisk executed a brilliant financial maneuver by converting Erie Railroad bonds into new shares of stock. The Erie board authorized $5 million in convertible bonds

sources.title: The Erie War: Vanderbilt vs Gould, Titans Fight For Control

facts.claim: The newly issued Erie shares were sold on the market and bought by Vanderbilt's own agents before their origin was suspected.
facts.quote: Fisk's new shares were thrown upon the market, and bought by Vanderbilt's agents before their origin was suspected.

facts.claim: In March 1868 Judge George Barnard issued an injunction freezing Erie's stock issuance and appointing a receiver; Drew left for New Jersey, and Gould and Fisk crossed the Hudson by rowboat with several million dollars removed from the Erie vault and took refuge at the Taylor Hotel in Jersey City, nicknamed 'Fort Taylor'.
facts.quote: Drew fled immediately for the safety of New Jersey. Gould and Fisk delayed, but when it became clear that their arrest was imminent, they rushed to Canal Street and secured a rowboat and crew. After nearly capsizing in choppy waters with several million dollars hastily removed from the Erie Railway's vault, they crossed the Hudson and took refuge at the Taylor Hotel

sources.title: The Erie War: Vanderbilt vs Gould, Titans Fight For Control

facts.claim: Accounts of the financial outcome differ: one history estimates the Erie was 'milked' of no less than $9 million in the final settlement, while another states Vanderbilt lost more than $7 million but recovered most of it from Gould under threat of litigation.
facts.quote: Vanderbilt lost more than $7 million in his attempt to gain control over Erie Railway Company, although Gould later returned most of the money under threat of litigation.

sources.title: The Erie War: Vanderbilt vs Gould, Titans Fight For Control

facts.claim: Vanderbilt's attempt to gain control of the Erie was defeated when the Erie directors flooded the market with newly converted shares, which his brokers bought before realising where they came from.
facts.quote: Fisk's new shares were thrown upon the market, and bought by Vanderbilt's agents before their origin was suspected.

sources.title: The Erie War: Vanderbilt vs Gould, Titans Fight For Control

connections.claim: Vanderbilt was opposed in the 1868 Erie contest by Erie treasurer Daniel Drew, who with Gould and Fisk issued the new shares that defeated Vanderbilt's buying.
connections.quote: Drew, Gould, and Fisk executed a brilliant financial maneuver by converting Erie Railroad bonds into new shares of stock.

connections.claim: Histories report that Vanderbilt recovered most of his Erie losses from Gould under threat of litigation after the 1868 contest.
connections.quote: Gould later returned most of the money under threat of litigation.

sources.title: The Erie War: Vanderbilt vs Gould, Titans Fight For Control

connections.claim: Fisk was one of the Erie directors whose newly issued shares were bought by Vanderbilt's agents during the 1868 Erie War.
connections.quote: Fisk's new shares were thrown upon the market, and bought by Vanderbilt's agents before their origin was suspected.

openQuestions: Site claim tested: the page says $10 million of convertible bonds were converted into roughly 100,000 shares; the sources found give $5 million of bonds and about 50,000 shares (Financial History magazine, American-Rails). Figures differ by a factor of two; owner should check against a documented history of the 1868 issues.

Site claim tested: the Albany bribery account (Gould with a satchel of $500,000) traces to Gustavus Myers and appears in the sources only as a quotation of Myers; no legislative record, bill number or vote count was found.
Site claim tested: the flight to Jersey City and 'Fort Taylor' is supported; the amount taken ($6-7 million on the page) is given only as 'several million dollars' in the sources found.
The page calls Vanderbilt a 'robber baron who attempted to corner Erie shares'; the sources describe an attempt to buy control rather than a technical corner.
